question: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
principle: Race on the racetrack, walk on ice

raiseTranscript.text: In my first internship I spent two days writing unit tests and a full design doc for a one-off script that pulled data for a weekly report. My manager asked why it was late and I realized the script would only run twice before being replaced.
I shipped a quick version, then asked my mentor how to judge when to add tests. He said match effort to lifetime of the code. Next task I asked upfront and finished in hours instead of days.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Intern wrote full design doc and tests for a throwaway weekly report script
Took two days; manager flagged delay
Quote: 'I realized the script would only run twice before being replaced'
Follow-up: Asked mentor how to judge effort; now asks upfront on new tasks
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on judgment. Candidate owned a clear over-application on an individual task, described the concrete cost (two-day delay on a two-run script), and showed immediate behavior change after feedback. The quote about asking upfront demonstrates coachability at the right scope for a junior. No evidence of repeated mistakes or defensiveness. Biggest strength is linking the lesson to a repeatable question they now ask.

lowerTranscript.text: I once spent a week building a full requirements doc for a small internal tool because the template said to. It delayed the project but at least everything was documented.
Did you change anything after that?
Not really, the template is still required so I just follow it now.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Spent a week on requirements doc for small internal tool per template
Delayed project; no change in approach
Quote: 'the template is still required so I just follow it now'
Follow-up: No evidence of adapting rigor to context
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on judgment. Candidate describes the over-rigor but shows no ownership or learning, defaulting to 'the template is required.' The story stays at the individual task level with no follow-up action or coachability signal. Biggest gap is absence of any adjustment after the delay, which is the core skill this principle tests for juniors.

raiseTranscript.text: Our team was integrating with another squad's API. I pushed for a full RFC, architecture review, and load tests even though the change was a simple field addition. It added three weeks.

After the second week I talked to the other lead, realized the risk was low, and we switched to a lightweight review. We shipped in four days and I updated our team checklist to ask 'blast radius?' before choosing process.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Pushed full RFC and load tests for simple API field addition across teams
Added three weeks; then switched to lightweight review after talking to other lead
Quote: 'we switched to a lightweight review. We shipped in four days'
Follow-up: Updated team checklist with 'blast radius?' question
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on judgment. Senior candidate recognized cross-team over-rigor, took initiative to adjust mid-stream, and institutionalized a lightweight check for the team. The three-week delay and four-day recovery provide clear before/after metrics. The blast-radius question shows influence without authority. Biggest strength is turning a personal mistake into a team process improvement.

lowerTranscript.text: We over-engineered a cross-team migration with full reviews and sign-offs. It dragged on but leadership wanted the process so we kept going.
What did you do differently later?
I still recommend the same process because it protects us from surprises.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Over-engineered cross-team migration with full reviews despite low risk
Quote: 'I still recommend the same process because it protects us from surprises'
Follow-up: No evidence of adjusting for context or influencing lighter process
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on judgment. Candidate describes a multi-week delay on a cross-team effort but shows no attempt to calibrate rigor or influence a better path. The response defends the process rather than owning the mismatch. Biggest gap is lack of any learning or adjustment, which is expected at senior level where cross-team calibration matters.

raiseTranscript.text: At company scale we mandated a full security review and threat model for every feature launch. A small marketing site change got caught in the process and delayed a revenue campaign by six weeks.
What changed at the org level?

I worked with security and legal to create a tiered review matrix based on data sensitivity and customer impact. We reduced review time on low-risk work by 80 percent while keeping high-risk items rigorous. The matrix is now used across three product groups.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Mandated full security review for every launch including low-risk marketing site
Quote: 'We reduced review time on low-risk work by 80 percent while keeping high-risk items rigorous'
Follow-up: Created tiered matrix now used across three product groups
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on judgment. Executive candidate owned an org-wide over-application that hit revenue, then drove a structural fix (tiered matrix) with measurable impact across multiple groups. The six-week delay and 80 percent reduction give concrete scale. Biggest strength is strategic trade-off thinking that preserved necessary rigor while removing friction at the right places.

lowerTranscript.text: We applied heavy compliance reviews to all initiatives after a past incident. Some projects slowed but it was the safe call.
We kept the reviews because the risk was too high to change.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you applied more rigor than a situation needed and slowed things down unnecessarily. What did you learn?
Applied heavy compliance reviews org-wide after past incident
Quote: 'We kept the reviews because the risk was too high to change'
Follow-up: No evidence of strategic recalibration or leverage
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on judgment. Candidate describes an org-level slowdown but offers no strategic re-evaluation or willingness to differentiate risk. The response treats the process as fixed rather than a lever to tune. Biggest gap is absence of long-term thinking or trade-off analysis expected at exec scope.

diagnostic.signal: Recognition of mismatch between rigor and risk

diagnostic.senior: Takes responsibility and adjusts with peers
diagnostic.exec: Takes responsibility and drives org change

diagnostic.junior: Asks clarifying question on next task

Creates durable policy with measured trade-offs
Treats heavy process as fixed despite scale cost
